readout_other: antidromic sensory nerve conduction latency (Teca EMG recorder); subcutaneous temperature by thermistor
direction_notes: Conduction latency of the superficial radial nerve shortened with a 1.2 C rise in subcutaneous temperature, equally for ultrasound and infrared; no mechanical effect of ultrasound was identified.

exposures.label: Continuous 1 MHz ultrasound to forearm over superficial radial nerve

target.label: superficial terminal branch of the radial nerve

timing.protocol_description: Ultrasound applied in circular motion with a 2-cm sound head until subcutaneous temperature rose 1.2 C, interrupted after each 0.3 C rise to record latency. Treatment lasted 5 to 20 minutes (mean 13.2 minutes). Infrared comparison given in a separate session.

source_quotes.n_subjects: Ten healthy adults were exposed to ultrasound and infrared on separate treatment sessions
source_quotes.n_sessions_per_subject: Group A received ultrasound during the first session and infrared during the second session.
source_quotes.exposures[0].fundamental_frequency_khz: at a frequency of 1 MHz continuous wave
source_quotes.exposures[0].unspecified_domain.ispta_w_: using 1 $. 0 \ \mathbf { W } / \mathbf { c m } ^ { 2 }$ at a frequency of 1 MHz continuous wave
source_quotes.exposures[0].timing.sonication_duration_: The duration of the ultrasound treatments varied from 5 to 20 minutes
source_quotes.exposures[0].unspecified_domain.isppa_w_: Ultrasound was administered to the forearm between the stimulating and recording electrodes in a circular fashion using 1 $. 0 \ \mathbf { W } / \mathbf { c m } ^ { 2 }$ at a frequency of 1 MHz continuous wave.

flags.reason: 1.0 W/cm2 is a clinical dial intensity; the paper does not say whether it is spatial-peak or spatial-average or temporal-average; placed under ispta as continuous wave.
Duration varied with rate of temperature rise; recorded as stated range.
Peripheral nerve stimulated percutaneously in forearm, not brain.
Latency fell with heating in both ultrasound and infrared conditions; authors attribute this to heat, not a specific ultrasound effect.
Infrared heating was used as a comparison modality; there was no sham ultrasound.
